---
name: address-pr-reviews
description: >-
  Address all review comments on a pull request. Use when a pull request has received review
  feedback that needs to be resolved.
argument-hint: The pull request number
---

Resolve every review comment on the pull request. When you finish, each comment has a reply that
matches what the pull request's head contains.

Read all reviews, review threads and pull request comments, including replies inside threads you
answered before. Account for each one so none is overlooked.

If any feedback is ambiguous or reveals knowledge gaps, conduct a /grilling session using the
/domain-modeling skill to clarify the intent before making changes. A question the reviewer asks
gets an answer in its thread.

Apply a suggested change as written. Fix only obvious typos and style formats in it, and say so in
the reply.

Reply in each comment's own thread as soon as its fix is pushed, naming the commit and what
changed, or the decision you made instead. When the fix changes the UI, show the result in the
reply with the `capture-ui-evidence` skill.

---
name: ai-attribution
description: >-
  Add AI attribution to everything published on the user's behalf. Use whenever you
  create an issue or pull request, comment on or reply to an issue, post a pull request review or
  inline review comment, reply to a review thread, or write a commit message.
---

Add AI attribution to everything you publish on the user's behalf. This includes issues,
pull requests, comments, replies, reviews, inline review comments, and commit messages, whether you
write them directly or through another skill. Never publish without the attribution.

Get the user's name from the git configuration. Take the model from your system prompt or runtime
configuration. Do not guess either one. If you cannot determine them, ask the user before
publishing.

Write the model's human-readable name, not its ID. Runtimes and sub-agents often report a slug
such as `openai-codex/gpt-6.1-sol:high` or `openrouter/glm-5.3-flash:auto`. Drop the provider
prefix and the thinking-level or routing suffix, then write what remains the way its vendor does,
such as `GPT-6.1-Sol`, `GLM-5.3-Flash`, or `Claude Sonnet 4.5`.

When you delegate publishing to a sub-agent, do not pass your own model name in its instructions.
The sub-agent may run on a different model, so tell it to determine its own model the same way and
attribute the work to that model.

End issues, pull requests, comments, and reviews with:

```markdown
---
<sub>This comment was added on behalf of <name> by AI (<model>).</sub>
```

Adapt the wording to what you are publishing, such as "This issue was created", "This pull
request was opened", "This review was posted", or "This reply was added". Keep the rest of the
footnote unchanged.

For pull request reviews, add the attribution to both the review body and every inline review
comment, since GitHub displays each inline comment in its own thread.

Attribute commits with a `Co-Authored-By` trailer instead of a footnote. Name the model and use its
vendor's no-reply address, such as `noreply@anthropic.com` for Claude models or
`noreply@email.openai.com` for OpenAI models.

When editing a post or amending a commit, keep a single attribution naming the current model.

---
name: capture-ui-evidence
description: >-
  Show reviewers a UI change with screenshots or screen recordings attached where they read it.
  Use when opening a pull request with UI changes or responding to review feedback with a fix
  that changes the UI.
---

Let the reviewer judge a UI change without checking out the branch. When you finish, the pull
request or review reply shows every meaningful visual change with screenshots or recordings that
render inline on GitHub.

Capture the running application using the code under review. Mockups and design files don't
count, because they can't show a bug you introduced. Recapture evidence after any change that
could affect the appearance or behavior it shows. Use realistic data so the layout looks the
way users will see it, and keep secrets, tokens, and personal data out of the frame.

Match the media to the change. Use screenshots for static changes, such as a resized table, a
moved button, or new copy. Crop them to the affected area, leaving enough of the page around it
that the reviewer can tell where it is. For behavior changes, use a short recording showing the
interaction and its visible result. Include the starting state when the reviewer needs it to
understand the change. Add a before and after pair when the difference is too subtle to spot
alone. Skip changes with nothing visible to show.

Give each image alt text that describes the state it shows, such as "save button in the page
header". Put a recording alone in its paragraph so GitHub renders it as a player rather than a
link. Say in a sentence what the reviewer should look at when it isn't obvious.

Upload evidence as GitHub attachments rather than committing it to the repository. Keep review
replies in their original threads, because that is where the reviewer expects the answer. If
attachments cannot appear there, link to a conversation comment containing the evidence.

Read [GitHub attachments](github-attachments.md) when uploading evidence to a description,
conversation comment, or review-thread reply.

Verify that every attachment uploaded successfully, renders correctly, and appears next to the
text it supports. Delete the local captures only after verifying the published evidence.

---
name: code-review
description: >-
  Review a change against the project's standards and its spec, and check that its tests would
  catch regressions. Use when an agent needs independent feedback on work in progress, such as
  before opening a pull request, or when the user wants a change reviewed locally. To post the
  findings on a pull request, use `review-pr`.
argument-hint: "Optional: the change to review and the issue or spec it implements"
---

Review the change on three axes, each defined in its own reference:

- [Standards](standards-axis.md): does the code follow the project's conventions and best
  practices?
- [Spec](spec-axis.md): does the code do what the originating issue or spec asked for?
- [Tests](tests-axis.md): would the tests fail if the changed behavior were wrong?

The change is whatever the caller names: a branch, a pull request, or the uncommitted work in
progress. When nothing is named, review the current branch against its base.

Run each axis in its own `reviewer` agent, in parallel, so no axis pollutes another's context and
none shares the author's. Pass each reviewer its axis reference as written, with the reporting
rules below, instead of summarizing them, so every reviewer applies the same definition. You
don't need to read the axis references yourself.

Each reviewer opens its report with its exact model ID, copied from its system prompt or runtime
configuration. If neither names a model, it says so rather than guessing. Keep each axis summary
under 200 words. Keep individual findings concise without omitting evidence needed to act on them.

Each finding states the problem, why it matters, and a concrete remedy, with its file and line
when applicable. Distinguish demonstrated problems from uncertain concerns.

Return the findings to the caller grouped by axis, each axis with the model that reviewed it.
Don't merge or rerank findings across the axes, so one never masks another. Publish nothing:
the review leaves no trace on the pull request, the issue, or the commit history.

---
name: craft-pr
description: >-
  Open a pull request a reviewer can follow on its own, or tidy an open one, without changing
  behavior. Use whenever you are about to open a pull request from the current branch, or when the
  user wants to clean up or reorganize an existing pull request.
---

Turn the current work into a pull request a reviewer can follow on its own. They should see what
the change is for, which files matter, and where the risks are, without reconstructing the author's
intent from the raw diff. Cut the noise while leaving the behavior alone.

Start from the existing pull request, or open one if none exists. Read its commits, full diff,
changed paths, generated and mechanical files, and description. Note everything that slows a
reviewer down: noisy or tangled history, a stale or thin description, unrelated changes, mechanical
edits mixed with behavioral ones, missing test context, or no obvious place to start reading.

Rewrite history only when the user asked for it or approved your plan. If the history needs work,
propose the new commit structure first. Aim for commits that each hold one meaningful change and,
where practical, can be reviewed on their own. Avoid changing code unless it is necessary to make
the pull request accurate and reviewable. When the code itself does not need to change, improve
the description and reviewer guidance instead.

The description must start with a brief summary of the change and, when available, explain why the
change was needed. It should accurately describe what the change does, distinguish core files from
generated or mechanical ones, and cover meaningful risks, migration and rollout steps. Link issues,
design docs, dashboards, or other context when they explain the intent. It should also include a
review guide that walks the reviewer through the change. Name the file to start with, usually the
one that holds the core idea, such as a new type, interface, or entry point. Then give the order to
read the rest. For each stop, say in a sentence what that part does and how it connects to the
surrounding code, such as who calls it, what data passes through it, and what it replaces when
relevant. Point to the code that needs the closest look and the files that are safe to skim. Size
the guide to the change. A small pull request may need only a line or two. When the change affects
the UI, show it with the `capture-ui-evidence` skill.

Give each section a Markdown heading so reviewers can find it at a glance. Keep the visible
description to 30 lines or fewer. When the full description would run longer than 30 lines, keep
the summary and the reason for the change visible, and move the longer sections, such as the
review guide or file breakdown, into collapsible `<details>` blocks, each with a `<summary>` line
saying what it holds. Leave a blank line after `<summary>` so GitHub renders the Markdown inside.
Keep the attribution footnote outside any collapsed block.

Never present a behavior change as cleanup. If the pull request is too big, or mixes unrelated
concerns so badly that tidying cannot make it reviewable, recommend splitting it instead of
polishing around the problem.

Before you finish, confirm that the pull request still represents the intended changes and that
nothing changed behavior by accident.

---
name: implement-issue
description: >-
  Implement a single issue end-to-end, from code changes through pull request, CI, and code
  review, until the pull request is merged. Use when the user wants one ready-for-agent issue
  picked and implemented, or says things like "dispatch the next one", "implement a ready
  issue", or "work the queue". To implement every sub-issue of a specification, use
  `implement-spec`.
argument-hint: "Optional: the issue number to implement, or leave this blank to auto-pick."
---

Take a single issue from open to a merged pull request without pausing for user sign-off.

When no issue number is provided, select the highest-ranked issue that is open, labeled
`ready-for-agent`, unassigned, and has no open `blocked_by` dependency. If an issue number is
provided and the issue has sub-issues, select the topmost of those sub-issues that meets the
same criteria. Otherwise, use the provided issue, and stop and report why if it is closed,
assigned, or blocked. If no eligible issue can be found, stop and report that.

Self-assign the issue before starting, so no one else picks it up.

Read the issue and all its comments. If it has a parent, read enough of the parent and its
comments to understand the context the issue depends on. Plan the implementation. For code changes
identify the seams under test; seams gathered from the issue and its acceptance criteria count as
confirmed.

Change only what the issue requires. All agents writing code use the `tdd` skill. Run the tests,
linters, and formatters locally before reporting the work as done. You can use sub-agents when
useful. If you do, give them the issue, the relevant parent context, your plan, and these rules.

Before opening the pull request, run the `code-review` skill against the issue and the complete
implementation, including branch commits, staged, unstaged, and untracked implementation files.
Evaluate each finding on its merits. Make the smallest changes necessary to address valid concerns,
avoid scope creep, and push back on findings that you disagree with.

Allow up to three review rounds. The first reviews the complete implementation; subsequent rounds
focus on changes made since the previous review and any outstanding findings. Extend the limit to
five rounds only when unresolved findings involve security, permissions, authentication, or data
loss. You may stop the reviews early when only nits or no actionable findings remain. After
addressing findings, run the tests, linters, and formatters locally before reviewing again. Continue
until no findings remain that warrant changes or the round limit is reached.

Then open a clear, concise, reviewable pull request with a `Closes: #<N>` trailer. Briefly explain
any declined or unresolved findings and their technical rationale in the pull request description.
See the pull request through until it is merged. After every push, check CI and fix any failures
your changes caused. If three consecutive pushes don't turn CI green, stop and report it as a
blocker. Leave pre-existing and environmental failures alone, and never make CI pass by weakening
or deleting a test.

Address every review or comment on the pull request with the `address-pr-reviews` skill. Run the
relevant tests, linters, and formatters locally before each push, and get CI green again.

Keep watching the pull request for new comments and further review rounds, and repeat the same
cycle for each one, until the pull request is merged.

Always add AI attribution to every commit, pull request, review comment, and reply, including
those written by sub-agents.

Never merge the pull request without the user's explicit consent.

Stop early and report a blocker when the issue and its context aren't enough to implement it,
when a decision is needed that they don't answer, or when a failure blocks progress and can't
be fixed safely.

---
name: implement-spec
description: >-
  Implement a specification issue end-to-end by running `implement-issue` on each of its
  sub-issues in dependency order. Use when the user wants a whole spec or parent issue
  implemented, including all of its sub-issues. To implement a single issue, use
  `implement-issue`.
argument-hint: "The specification or parent issue number"
---

Take the specification issue from open to fully implemented. Each sub-issue is one unit of
work, handled by the `implement-issue` skill. That skill defines how a single issue is
implemented, reviewed, and merged. This one decides which sub-issues run and when.

Start by reading the specification issue and all its comments, then every sub-issue and its
comments. Use the `blocked_by` relationships to work out the dependencies. Follow the ordering
those dependencies require, and add no other except the exemplar below.

When several sub-issues make the same kind of change, such as rewrites that share a style or a
contract, run one of them first as the exemplar and hold the rest until the user has reviewed it.
The user's review of the first one sets rules every later one needs, and running them all at once
means each repeats the same mistakes. Unrelated sub-issues still run alongside it.

Run `implement-issue` on every sub-issue that is currently unblocked, passing it the sub-issue
number. Unblocked sub-issues can run in parallel, each in its own sub-agent with its own full
lifecycle. Give each sub-agent the rules the user's reviews have set so far, and pass a new one to
every sub-agent still working as soon as the user states it.

Keep watching the open pull requests. When the user merges one, re-check the sub-issues and run
`implement-issue` on any that are now unblocked. Keep going until every applicable sub-issue's
pull request is merged.

When `implement-issue` reports a blocker on a sub-issue, stop and report it rather than skip
the sub-issue.

When every sub-issue's pull request is merged, run the `scope-completeness-review` skill on the
specification issue. Report each completed sub-issue with its pull request and status, the
review's outcome, and any gaps or proposed follow-up issues without acting on them.

---
name: review-pr
description: >-
  Review a pull request against the project's standards, its spec, and its tests, and post the
  findings on it as a pull request review. Use when the user asks to "review this PR" or wants a
  second pair of eyes on a pull request they are reviewing.
argument-hint: "The pull request number"
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Review the pull request with the `code-review` skill, then post its findings as one pull request
review, so each finding gets a thread the author can answer.

Post the review as a comment. Approving or requesting changes is the user's verdict, not yours.

Put each finding tied to a line in an inline comment on that line. In the review body, summarize
the findings under `## Standards`, `## Spec`, and `## Tests`, and give in full the ones with no line
to comment on. If an axis was skipped, say why under its heading. Under each heading, name the model
that reviewed that axis by its human-readable name, such as `GPT-6.1-Sol` rather than
`openai-codex/gpt-6.1-sol:high`. End the body with the finding count for each axis and its worst
finding, when any exist.

Write for the pull request's author: direct, specific, technical and courteous.

---
name: scope-completeness-review
description: >-
  Check that a parent or spec issue's original scope is fully built, across its closed sub-issues
  and the code, and close the issue when it is. Use when a parent issue is ready for a final
  completeness check, or the user asks whether an issue is really done.
argument-hint: "The issue number"
---

Confirm that everything the issue asked for exists in the code before closing it. A closed
sub-issue claims coverage but doesn't prove it, so check each claim against the current code.

Read the original issue, including its acceptance criteria, requirements, and comments, then read
every closed sub-issue created to address it. Treat each acceptance criterion or requirement as a
separate requirement. For each, find the sub-issue that addresses it, if any, and read the code to
confirm it does what the requirement asks.

Build a coverage checklist with one row per requirement, listing the requirement, the sub-issue
that addresses it, the relevant code, and its status. The status is covered, partial, missing, or
divergent when the code does something other than what the issue asked for.

If every requirement is covered, post the checklist as a comment on the issue and close it as
completed. Otherwise, leave the issue open, report the gaps, and propose a follow-on issue for each
one that describes the remaining work.

---
name: windbag
description: >-
  Cut verbose prose so readers read it to the end. Use during code review and before opening or
  updating a pull request, on the code comments and docs in the diff, the pull request body, the
  bodies of issues it links, and the branch's commit messages. Also use when the user asks to cut
  verbose prose, shorten documentation, or make text more readable.
---

Your job is to cut every comment, doc passage, and sentence its reader doesn't need, and to
shorten what remains. Long prose gets skipped, and skipped text informs no one. Every decision
here, including each tie you break, answers one question: will a reader read this to the end?
When in doubt, cut. You're done when every accepted finding is applied, protected text is
untouched, and no information the reader needs has been lost.

The scope is what the caller names: files, a branch, or a pull request. For a branch or pull
request, review the docs and code comments in the diff, the pull request body, relevant linked
issues, and the branch's commit messages. When nothing is named, use the current branch against
its base.

Split the scope into small batches and spawn one `sonic` subagent per batch, in parallel. Sonic
runs on a small model that loses track of the catalogue as its input grows, so size each batch by
what it reads: about 100 lines of prose, from files of about 1,000 lines in total. A big file with
few comments still fills the context, so split it into batches by line range. Keep each kind of
prose in its own batches: comments and docs, the pull request and issue bodies, and commit
messages. Keep every comment, paragraph, and section whole within one batch, since its reader
reads all of it.

Each subagent acts as an independent reader whose goal is to find prose that can be removed,
shortened, or restructured so readers are more likely to read it to the end. Have each subagent
follow [rules.md](rules.md), examine every applicable pattern in its catalogue, and report
actionable findings with the evidence required by the rules.

Each subagent works in a fresh context and fetches its own text and diffs. Give it only the path
to the rules, the files, headings, line ranges, or commits in its batch, and the base and head
refs or the pull request and issue numbers, so it can search the rest of the scope for copies.
Tell it that a report with an unverified list, a check handed back, or a pattern name outside the
catalogue is invalid.

Before judging a report, check it as a whole. When it's invalid by the brief's terms, verifies
instead of cutting, skips the catalogue, or misreads the scope, rerun that subagent once and name
what went wrong. Don't rerun it again. Judge the findings of both reports, so a finding the rerun
drops is still judged.

Judge each finding on its own. Reject one only by citing the rule it breaks and the evidence that
it does; a ground the rules don't state isn't one. Findings that share a pattern or a file are
still judged one at a time, and none is rejected as part of a group.

Before applying, check that every place an accepted finding says a fact lives survives the other
accepted cuts. When two cuts each rely on the other's copy, drop the one that deletes the copy
where readers look first.

Apply the accepted findings. Edit files directly, preserving their meaning and the information
readers need. When changing a comment reveals that the code itself needs clarification, make the
smallest necessary code change, then build and run the tests.

Apply commit message findings to unmerged commits. Obtain approval before rewriting published
history or force-pushing. Edit pull request descriptions directly. Review linked issues for
context, but do not rewrite their bodies merely because the pull request references them. Only
edit an issue when it is explicitly within the requested editing scope, preserving its agreed
requirements and intent.

Summarize meaningful changes, where relocated information ended up, each rejected finding with
the rule it rests on, and any unresolved work.

---
name: writing-skills
description: >-
  Write or edit text another agent will follow, such as a skill or agent instructions. Use when
  creating, rewriting, or reviewing agent-facing instructions.
---

Write for a capable agent that has never seen this project's history. Give it the outcome, the
rules it can't infer, and the moments it must stop for the user. Leave the mechanics to it.

Open with the goal and what done looks like in terms someone could verify. Then give each rule
the agent needs, one concern per short paragraph, with its reason when it isn't obvious. Say each
thing once.

Prefer descriptive over prescriptive guidance. A skill says what to do, not how to do it. Describe
the outcomes, constraints, and evidence of completion, and leave the approach to the agent.
Specify a tool, command, sub-agent, or sequence only when it is part of the requirement itself.

Cut what the agent already knows: how to find the repo, which command does a job, what a common
term means, that it should read the issue it was given, or that an API exists. Cut what its context
already provides, such as configuration loaded by the agent instructions. Cut sentences that
describe an older version, a removed script, or a transition state. When rewriting, keep a sentence
because the agent needs it, not because the old text had it.

Keep the skill to its own job. When another skill covers part of the work, hand that part over by
name instead of restating its rules. Don't plan work the user will do, run another skill's review,
or describe what the platform does on its own.

Do not require delegation by default. Let the agent decide whether sub-agents help unless separate
context, independent judgement, parallel execution, or another property of delegation is itself
part of the skill's design.

Ask the user when the agent cannot determine what to do or when the choice belongs to the user,
such as choosing between valid alternatives. Require confirmation before actions that are
immediately visible to others and difficult to undo, such as publishing a release. Describe each
stop where it happens rather than collecting gates up front. Everything else proceeds without one.

Ask for a report only when the user will act on it. Drop statements such as "this skill is
read-only", "say what you couldn't check", and closing next-step lines unless they change what the
user does. When the agent writes something people will read, such as an issue body or review
findings, say what tone or qualities the output should have when that isn't already obvious.

Use structure when the structure carries meaning. A checklist, table, named review axis, or output
shape is useful when downstream work depends on it or when it makes the result easier to verify.
Avoid structure that merely turns prose into ceremony.

Prefer rules that remain true across implementations. Avoid encoding incidental details from the
current repository, toolchain, or workflow unless changing that detail would change the skill's
intended behavior.

The frontmatter description says what the skill does and when to use it, never how, and matches
the body. Put long references such as templates or rubrics in their own file next to the skill,
and link each with one sentence explaining when to read it.

Write plain sentences. Avoid numbered procedures, command blocks, unnecessary output templates,
emphasis words such as MUST or NEVER, persona openers, and harness tool names. Keep lines under
100 characters.

These rules apply to agent-facing text. Documentation written for people, such as a README, keeps
its author's voice.

# skills

[![skills.sh](https://skills.sh/b/gringolito/skills)](https://skills.sh/gringolito/skills)

AI skills for common tasks — a collection of reusable skills for AI agents that provide procedural knowledge to help them accomplish specific tasks more effectively.

## Installation

Install all skills from this repository using the [skills.sh](https://skills.sh) CLI:

```sh
npx skills add gringolito/skills
```

This will install all skills and make them available to your AI agent.

## Skills

| Skill | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [address-pr-reviews](./skills/address-pr-reviews/) | Address review comments on pull requests |
| [ai-attribution](./skills/ai-attribution/) | Mark issues, pull requests, comments, reviews, and commits written on the user's behalf with a footnote naming the AI model that wrote them |
| [capture-ui-evidence](./skills/capture-ui-evidence/) | Show reviewers UI changes with screenshots or recordings attached to the pull request or review reply |
| [code-review](./skills/code-review/) | Review a change against the project's standards and spec, check that its tests would catch regressions, and return the findings |
| [craft-pr](./skills/craft-pr/) | Craft the current work into a clean, reviewable pull request without changing its behavior |
| [implement-issue](./skills/implement-issue/) | Take a single issue through implementation, PR, CI, and code review until the PR is merged |
| [implement-spec](./skills/implement-spec/) | Implement every sub-issue of a specification by running `implement-issue` on each in dependency order |
| [review-pr](./skills/review-pr/) | Review a pull request with `code-review` and post the findings on it as a review |
| [scope-completeness-review](./skills/scope-completeness-review/) | Check that a parent or spec issue's scope is fully built in the code, and close the issue once it is |
| [windbag](./skills/windbag/) | Cut verbose comments, docs, pull request and issue bodies, and commit messages during review so readers read them to the end |
| [writing-skills](./skills/writing-skills/) | Write or edit skills and other instructions meant for agents to follow |

## Review workflow

`code-review` returns actionable findings without publishing them. Each axis summary stays under
200 words; finding details retain the evidence needed to act on them. `review-pr` publishes those
findings as a comment-only pull request review.

Before opening a pull request, `implement-issue` reviews the complete implementation, including
committed branch work and staged, unstaged, or untracked implementation files. It fixes agreed
findings and explains declined findings with brief technical reasons in the pull request description.

# GitHub attachments

For a pull request description or a comment on the main conversation, the GitHub CLI's
`--attach` flag uploads each file and rewrites local paths in the Markdown body to the uploaded
URLs.

Review thread replies have no attach option. Upload each file to GitHub's user attachments
endpoint on `uploads.github.com`, the same one the CLI uses, passing the repository ID, file
name, and content type. Embed the URL it returns in the reply. That endpoint is undocumented.
If it fails, post the media on the main conversation with `--attach`, and reply in the thread
with a link to that comment.

# Spec axis

Does the code do what the originating issue or spec asked for?

Review the change against the issue or spec it implements: the one the caller names, or the
issue a pull request closes. Failing both, use the pull request description when it defines the
expected behavior. If nothing provides a useful specification, skip this axis and say so.

Look for requirements that are missing or only partially implemented, behavior that was not
requested (scope creep), and requirements that appear implemented but are implemented incorrectly.
Cite the requirement behind each finding. For scope creep, point to the code nobody asked for.

# Standards axis

Does the code follow the project's conventions and best practices?

Identify the project's documented coding conventions and architectural decisions, including files
such as `CODING_STANDARDS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, and ADRs under common locations such as
`docs/adrs/`, `docs/decisions/`, or `adrs/`. Leave test quality and testing conventions to the
tests axis.

Every applicable ADR that hasn't been superseded is a project standard. Use it as precedent for
implementation choices, especially when it sets a cross-cutting constraint or a preferred pattern.
Its historical context and rejected alternatives are not requirements. Departing from an ADR is a
violation even when the code is clean. If the departure looks intentional, recommend a new ADR that
supersedes the old one instead of reverting the code. An architectural choice no ADR covers is a
candidate for a new one.

Use the code smells below when evaluating code design. They apply even when the project documents
nothing, but a documented standard or ADR overrides them. Apply only relevant smells a reviewer
could reasonably act on and that are not already enforced by tooling.

## Code smells

From Fowler's _Refactoring_, chapter 3. Smells are judgement calls, so report each one by name as
"possible Feature Envy". A violation of a documented standard or ADR is reported plainly.

| Code smell | Description | Fix suggestion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mysterious Name | A function, variable, or type whose name doesn't reveal what it does or holds | Rename it. If no honest name comes to mind, the design is unclear |
| Duplicated Code | The same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file of the change | Extract the shared shape and call it from both |
| Feature Envy | A method uses another object's data more than its own | Move it onto the data it envies |
| Data Clumps | The same few fields or parameters keep travelling together | Bundle them into one type |
| Primitive Obsession | A primitive or string stands in for a domain concept | Give the concept its own small type |
| Repeated Switches | The same `switch` or `if` cascade on the same type recurs across the change | Replace it with polymorphism, or with one map both sites share |
| Shotgun Surgery | One logical change forces scattered edits across many files | Gather what changes together into one module |
| Divergent Change | One file or module changes for several unrelated reasons | Split it so each part changes for one reason |
| Speculative Generality | Abstractions, parameters, or hooks serve needs the spec doesn't have | Delete them until a real need shows up |
| Message Chains | The caller walks a long `a.b().c().d()` chain | Hide the walk behind one method on the first object |
| Middle Man | A class or function mostly delegates onward | Cut it and call the real target directly |
| Refused Bequest | A subclass or implementer ignores or overrides most of what it inherits | Drop the inheritance and use composition |

# Tests axis

Would the tests fail if the changed behavior were wrong?

Review whether the tests would catch meaningful regressions in behavior the change adds or
alters. Consider added, modified, deleted, and existing tests, as well as tests that should
have been added but weren't. Judge the tests, not the implementation. A production defect shows
up here only as the missing or weak test that let it through.

Follow the project's documented testing conventions and established patterns, including
test strategy ADRs. They take precedence over the guidance below on test level, structure, and
smells. A test that ignores an established pattern is a finding even when it works. If the change
has no testable behavior, skip this axis and say so. If the project has no tests, report that once
rather than listing every untested behavior.

For each behavior the change adds or alters, find the test that protects it and ask whether a
plausible implementation mistake would make it fail. Weigh how much protection each behavior needs
by the change's risk. Check meaningful boundary values, error paths, and requirements from the
spec. When there is no spec, review against the contracts evident in the change and say so. For
bug fixes, verify that the tests would fail without the fix. Judge assertions by what they prove,
not test names, passing results, or coverage numbers.

Look for missing or weak assertions, expected values derived from the implementation under
test, mocks or fixtures that hide the behavior being verified, and tests that mostly assert on
their own mocks. Deleted or disabled tests, weakened assertions, and updated snapshots or golden
files each need a reason the change supplies. Without one, report them as possibly bent to fit
the implementation.

Check that each test runs at a level that can expose the likely failure. Prefer focused tests for
isolated logic and tests that cross real integration points for integration behavior. Recommend
broader tests only when existing tests cannot catch a concrete failure.

Use the test smells below when evaluating test quality. Apply only relevant smells that are not
already enforced by tooling, and distinguish subjective smells from violations of documented
conventions.

For each finding, describe a plausible regression the current tests would miss and the
smallest test or assertion that would catch it. Report a changed behavior no test covers as a
coverage gap, not a smell. Don't ask for tests that duplicate existing coverage, exercise private
implementation details, or cover every changed line.

When executing tests or trying mutations would resolve uncertainty, use an isolated copy so
the other reviewers' working tree remains unchanged. Distinguish observed results from
conclusions based on code inspection.

## Test smells

Mostly from Meszaros's _xUnit Test Patterns_. Smells are judgement calls, so report each one by
name as "possible Erratic Test". A violation of a documented testing convention is reported
plainly.

| Test smell | Description | Fix suggestion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assertion-Free Test | The test runs code but asserts nothing meaningful, or asserts only that no exception was thrown | Assert on the observable outcome the behavior promises |
| Overspecified Test | The test asserts on implementation details such as call order, private state, or exact mock interactions | Assert on outputs and observable effects so refactoring doesn't break it |
| Eager Test | One test verifies several unrelated behaviors | Split it so each test has one reason to fail |
| Assertion Roulette | Many assertions whose failure output doesn't say which expectation broke | Split the test or add messages that name the expectation |
| Obscure Test | The setup buries what is being tested and why the expected value is right | Name the scenario, keep only relevant setup, and derive expected values visibly |
| Mystery Guest | The test depends on an external file, fixture, or environment the reader can't see | Inline the data or name the fixture so its relevance is obvious |
| General Fixture | A shared setup builds far more than any single test needs | Give each test the minimal fixture it uses |
| Conditional Test Logic | `if`, loops, or `try` inside a test decide what gets asserted | Make each path its own test, or use a parameterized test |
| Erratic Test | The outcome depends on time, randomness, ordering, sleeps, concurrency, or the network | Inject clocks and seeds, isolate state, and wait on conditions instead of durations |
| Interacting Tests | Tests share mutable state, so one passes or fails depending on another | Reset or isolate state per test |
| Test Code Duplication | The same setup or assertion shape is copied across tests, hiding what differs between them | Extract a helper, builder, or parameterized case that keeps the differences visible |
| Test Logic in Production | Production code gains flags, hooks, or branches that exist only for tests | Move the seam to a proper dependency injection point |

# Windbag rules

One question decides every finding: will a reader read this to the end? Long prose gets skipped,
and skipped text informs no one. Windbag cuts unnecessary prose, and when in doubt, it cuts.
Subagents use these rules to find what to cut and what to restructure. The main agent uses them to
judge findings and apply fixes.

## The subagent

Read like a copy editor with a red pen and a word budget. Every sentence is guilty until it earns
its place. Hunt for cuts, and prefer deleting a piece whole to shortening it.

Make each finding a concrete cut: the exact words to delete, or the text that replaces them, so
the main agent only decides yes or no. Edit nothing. Settle every check yourself: a report that
lists unverified items, says it didn't check something, or leaves a decision to the main agent is
invalid and gets rerun, so settle the check or drop the finding. Leave out any finding another
rule here rules out, such as one touching protected text.

Work in this order, and finish each step before starting the next:

1. Fetch the prose your brief points to and the diff it belongs to. Read only the ranges your brief
   names and the code a cut depends on, and search for copies with a text search instead of
   opening whole files.
2. Cut pass: make every piece in your batch earn its place against the cut patterns in the
   catalogue. Pieces over budget get the hardest look.
3. Reference pass: check references and claims only in what survives the cut pass, as described
   in Reading the code.

## Scope

A comment, paragraph, or section that the change touches is in scope as a whole for cuts, since
its reader reads all of it. Pieces the change doesn't touch are out of scope. When the user names
files instead of a change, all of their prose is in scope. The code is read only for lines the
change adds or rewrites.

## What the reader needs

The reader is a capable developer with solid technical knowledge and none of this work's context.
Explaining what they already know, such as a common term, a standard tool, or how a language
feature works, wastes their attention. What they can't know, such as why the change was made or a
constraint outside the code, stays.

Keep what the reader needs to do their job. Someone reading a commit message months later needs
what changed and why. A reviewer reading a pull request body needs what the change does, why,
and where to look. Whoever picks up an issue needs what done means. The next person changing
code needs what the code can't say. A doc's reader needs what to do and when.

A finding has to earn its place too. It either makes the reader more likely to finish, or it
points at something wrong.

Wording, extra examples, and minor facts can go. Precision stays: a qualifier that bounds a claim,
such as "or one before it" or "at most daily", is information. A fact the reader needs stays,
moves where that reader looks, such as into the code, a linked doc, or an issue, or already lives
there. A finding that would cut such a fact says where it already lives, when it does.

Cut whole sections before polishing sentences. Ask of each section whether its reader would miss
it, and drop it when they wouldn't, even when every sentence in it is fine. A pull request body
keeps what the change does, why, and where to start reading. Sections that retell an ADR or issue
the body links, list risks no reviewer would act on, report verification the checks already show,
or recount review rounds usually go. The same holds for paragraphs in docs and commit bodies.

Reference material, such as tables of variables, options, defaults, or values, is looked up rather
than read through. Keep every entry. Repetition in it can be merged, such as one table with a
column per service, but no value is dropped.

Some prose can't be cut without losing what the reader needs. Flag it for restructuring: the
point goes in the first sentence and details follow. A piece doing several jobs is split, or each
job moves to where its reader looks. In every piece over budget, read the first sentence of the
piece and of each section alone. When it doesn't carry the point, that is a finding, even when
nothing else is wrong.

## Length budgets

A budget is a ceiling. In a piece over budget, every sentence has to name a reason to stay: an
external constraint, a contract, or a fact the reader needs that lives nowhere else. The rest go,
and the piece comes down to budget unless the main agent names the reason for what's left over.
Under budget, cutting continues: the goal is the shortest text that still answers its reader, and
no text when it answers nothing.

| Kind | Budget |
| --- | --- |
| Commit subject | 72 characters |
| Commit body | about 80 words |
| Code comment | one line; a public API doc comment, one short paragraph |
| Doc or skill file section | about 150 words |
| Pull request body | about 150 words visible, with the rest in collapsed sections |
| Issue body | about 250 words |

## Protected text

Leave these alone, even when they are long:

- License and legal headers, and quoted legal or contract text.
- Verbatim quotes: error messages, logs, CLI output, and text quoted from people, specs, or
  other issues.
- Code, code blocks, commands, and configuration. The prose around them is fair game.
- Generated files and generated sections.
- Commit trailers, closing keywords such as `Closes #12`, and AI-attribution footers.
- Tool directives such as `//go:generate`, build tags, and `// prettier-ignore`. Lint and type
  suppressions follow the comment rules below.
- Frontmatter keys and other fields a tool reads, and sections that a template requires. Their
  content can be shortened, but the section stays.

## Code comments

A comment stays only when it names one of these reasons:

- Non-obvious behavior forced by an external dependency, platform, vendor, protocol, or data
  source we can't change.
- A public API contract, in a doc comment.
- An issue or RFC link that explains a constraint the code can't express.
- Open work: a surprise, rule, or shortcut whose code fix can't land in this change, as below.

Plausibly useful isn't a reason. A comment without one goes whole, however short, since no
comment beats one that tells the reader nothing. A comment with a reason comes down to its budget.

For suppressions such as `eslint-disable`, `@ts-ignore`, `@ts-expect-error`, `//nolint`, `# noqa`,
or `# type: ignore`, look up the rule. When it catches real bugs or protects correctness or
safety, the suppression goes, and the code changes so the rule passes.

A comment explaining a surprise in our own code goes, and the code changes so the behavior is
obvious without prose: a rename, an extracted function, a named constant, or a type. The finding
names the exact symbol. The change keeps behavior exactly as it is; one that would change behavior
is a separate fix, reported as open work. When the change reaches beyond the review's scope, it
is open work too, and the comment stays, shortened, until it lands.

A comment that states a rule for the code, such as "always sort before merging" or "never call
this twice", guards nothing: the next change can break the rule and still pass the build. Small
fixes often leave one behind. The comment goes, and the rule moves into something that fails when
it's broken, preferring a test or a function that does both steps. A type or assertion that would
reject input the code accepts today changes behavior, so it's open work, and the comment stays,
shortened, until it lands. When the fix already has such a test, the comment simply goes.

A comment that justifies a shortcut in our own code, such as a workaround, a duplicated block, a
skipped check, or "good enough for now", goes, and the right change replaces the shortcut. When
that change would alter behavior or reaches beyond the review's scope, it's open work: an issue
tracks it, and the comment shrinks to the issue link.

Commented-out code, banners, and TODOs without an issue link go. A TODO worth doing becomes an
issue.

## Reading the code

The cut pass reads the code for two questions only: whether a comment says what the code already
says, and whether a fact the reader needs already lives in the code.

The reference pass checks only what survives the cut pass. Check the file paths, symbols, flags,
options, environment variables, line numbers, versions, counts, and descriptions of current
behavior it names. Report each as stale, with what the code says instead, or as aging because it
pins a detail that changes as the code evolves. Either kind is cut or generalized when the reader
doesn't need it. A claim the code plainly contradicts, noticed during these checks, is a finding
too. Skip claims about a dependency instead of reading its source. A claim you can't confirm, or
one with no source, isn't a reason to cut; cut it only when its reader doesn't need it.

## Catalogue

Each finding names one of these patterns, and its cut follows the fix column. The cut pass uses
the first table and the reference pass the second.

| Pattern | Detection test | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unearned length | The piece is over budget, and a sentence anywhere in it names no reason to stay: an external constraint, a contract, or a fact that lives nowhere else. | Cut every sentence without a reason. Bring the piece to budget, or name the reason for any overage that remains. |
| Unneeded section | Remove the section or paragraph whole. The reader wouldn't miss it: it retells a linked ADR or issue, lists risks nobody acts on, reports verification the checks show, or recounts review. | Delete it whole. |
| Buried point | Read only the first sentence or line. It doesn't say what this is, what changed, or what to do. | Put the point first; details follow. Restructure. |
| Several jobs | The piece has more than one job, such as recording a decision and tracking open work, so each job's reader wades through the others. | Split it, or move each job to its home: the code, an ADR, an issue, a linked doc. Restructure. |
| Repeated statement | The same fact appears twice within one comment, section, message, or body, or restates a source the reader already has open, such as the issue a pull request links. | Keep it once, where the reader looks first. |
| Boilerplate | The same comment or passage appears in more than one file in scope, such as a header or setup note pasted into each. Search the scope for a comment's wording before keeping it. A copy counts even when each file could be read on its own. A fact about the object it annotates, such as a table's access policy, isn't boilerplate: each object's reader needs it there. | Keep one copy where readers look, such as the shared definition or a doc, and delete the rest. |
| Mirrored comment | A comment is copied into code that mirrors or restates other code, such as a migration's down section or a `CREATE OR REPLACE` that redefines an earlier object. | Delete the copy; the original keeps it. |
| Ceremony | Headings, bullets, tables, or template sections wrap a line or two of content, or say "N/A". | Write plain sentences. Drop empty sections no template requires. |
| Sprawl | A sentence makes more than one point, splits subject from verb with a long clause, or opens with a long lead-in. | Split it and put the subject and verb first. |
| Throat-clearing | A sentence announces what follows or that something is worth noting: "This PR...", "Note that", "It's worth mentioning". | Start with the claim. |
| Narration | The prose says what the code or diff visibly does, or walks through files the reader will open anyway. | Cut it. Keep the why and what the reader can't see. |
| Known basics | The prose explains something a capable developer already knows: a common term, a standard tool, or how a language feature works. | Cut it. |
| History | A doc, comment, or skill file tells how it got here: earlier designs, review rounds, "now", "no longer", "we changed". A commit message or pull request body that says what the change replaces is doing its job. | State the current state. History lives in git and the pull request thread. |
| Defensive justification | Rejected options nobody would propose, edge cases no reader will hit, or arguments for a choice nobody questioned. | Keep only the alternatives a reader would raise. |
| Enumeration over rule | Every instance is listed where one rule covers them, and readers read the list through rather than look things up in it. | State the rule. |
| Example overload | Several examples make one point. Drop all but the best one and the point still lands. | Keep the most representative example. |
| Situation-specific example | The example depends on one incident's details, so a reader can't map it to their own case. | Generalize it, or replace it with a representative one. |
| Restating comment | The comment says what the code or the name it annotates already says. | Delete it. |
| Surprise comment | The comment explains behavior of our own code that the code could make obvious. | Delete it and change the code, as in Code comments. |
| Unguarded rule | A comment states a rule the code doesn't enforce: "always", "never", "must", "make sure". | Delete it and enforce the rule in the code or a test, as in Code comments. |
| Excuse comment | A comment justifies a shortcut in our own code instead of fixing it: a workaround, a duplicate, a skipped check, "for now". | Delete it and make the right change, or open an issue, as in Code comments. |
| Dead text | Commented-out code, banners, or a TODO without an issue. | Delete it, opening an issue for a TODO worth doing. |
| Process chatter | The author reports what they ran, checked, or tried. | Keep test evidence a reviewer acts on, in a line. Cut the rest. |
| Restated subject | A body, section, or comment repeats its subject, heading, or the name it annotates. | Cut the repeat. |
| Needless contrast | "X, not Y" or "X, never Y" where Y only repeats X. | Drop the contrast unless it tells the reader something X doesn't. |
| Emphasis inflation | MUST, NEVER, IMPORTANT, bold, or capitals on things that aren't the main requirement. | Use plain words and let position carry emphasis. Keep "must" for real requirements. |
| Hedge or intensifier | very, really, just, basically, quite, clearly, should probably, or stacked qualifiers. | Cut it, unless it marks uncertainty the reader needs to know about. |
| Redundancy | Doubled words (each and every), implied categories (period of time), or modifiers the noun implies (final outcome). | Keep one word. |
| Wordy phrase | in order to, due to the fact that, at this point in time, is able to. | Use the short form. |
| Hidden verb | The action sits in a noun: perform validation of, make a decision about. | Use the verb. |
| Missing actor | A passive hides who acts, and the reader needs to know. | Name the actor. |

| Pattern | Detection test | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stale reference | A reference no longer matches the code. | Fix it if the reader needs it. Otherwise cut it. |
| Aging reference | An example names a file, symbol, flag, line number, version, count, or today's behavior that the reader doesn't need. | Describe the general case, or cut it. |
| False claim | A comment or doc says something the code plainly contradicts. | Correct the wrong part in no more words than it took, or report the code as open work. |

## Kinds of prose

A commit subject says what changed. The body says why, plus anything a reader of the log
wouldn't guess, including what the change replaces. A squash message describes the final
change, not each intermediate commit or review round, but the facts those commits record about
the final code stay unless the code or its docs already hold them.

A pull request body opens with what the change does and why. 

An issue body says what done means early. Its acceptance criteria don't restate its scope.

## Findings

Report findings only, leaving out summaries of what you checked or verified. Each finding gives:

- Location: file and line range, commit, pull request body, or issue number.
- Pattern: a catalogue name, exactly as written. A finding no pattern fits is left out.
- The cut: the exact words to delete, or the replacement text.
- What's wrong, in one sentence.
- Facts the reader needs in those words, and the exact file and line where each already lives, if
  anywhere. A finding that deletes a copy names the copy that stays the same way.
- Evidence from the code, for references, claims, and comment decisions.

## Fixes

Before cutting a piece, name the questions its reader comes with, such as what changed, why,
what to do, and what the rule is. Every answer survives, in the text or where the finding says it
lives. A piece's rule or main point never goes, even when its examples do. A fact stays only when
you can name its reader and what they'd lose without it, and then in as few words as it takes.

A replacement keeps the author's voice and formatting, such as line width and heading style. It
keeps whole sentences, since dropping articles, verbs, or connectives makes the reader decode
instead of read. It doesn't make the text longer, unless it corrects something wrong. A fact the
reader needs that lives nowhere else moves before it's cut. A replacement points by file, heading,
or symbol, without line numbers, since the same pass may move them. A code change keeps behavior,
builds, and passes the tests that cover it.
